items.title: The Hero Rats of Tanzania (full documentary) | FRONTLINE/World
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>Go inside an effort to train giant rats to sniff out deadly unexploded land mines — and save lives. (Aired 2007)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb 

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

Bart Weetjens founded a unique lab in Tanzania dedicated to training rats to sniff out deadly unexploded land mines — the legacy of countless bloody conflicts. Although dogs had traditionally been used to help humans detect mines, Weetjens, who had long felt a special bond with rodents, realized that African giant pouched rats were lighter, cheaper to care for, and less susceptible to tropical disease.

In “Hero Rats,” FRONTLINE/World reporter Alexis Bloom accompanied Weetjens to neighboring Mozambique to watch his organization’s trained rodents in action. She also visited a school there that was cleared of landmines with the help of the rats, allowing the children to resume their education and play without fear of stepping on a mine. The rats save human lives, Weetjens said, “and, yes, they are heroes, actually.”

“Tanzania: Hero Rats” was produced by Cassandra Herrman. It was reported by Alexis Bloom. For FRONTLINE/World, the coordinating producer was David Ritsher and the senior producer was Ken Dornstein. The founder and executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

items.title: Morocco's cannabis reform: Why small farmers are left behind | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Morocco's legalization of cannabis for medicinal purposes was welcomed by growers in the country. The promise of a better future, however, has yet to materialize for many small-scale farmers.

Cannabis farmers in northern Morocco are under pressure from changing climate conditions, with water shortages intensifying the already fierce competition in the sector. In Azila, a village that depends entirely on the drug trade for its livelihood, farmers are allowed to cultivate cannabis but are not authorized to trade it. Here in the Rif Mountains, thousands of families rely on cannabis cultivation, but most live under precarious conditions. The most productive land, where the plants grow best, belongs to a handful of large operators who are increasingly taking control of the business. Anyone who continues to sell the crop illegally risks imprisonment.
Many farmers support legalization because they hope it will enable them to live without a constant fear of prosecution. The government's legalization program, however, is progressing more slowly than expected, with fewer farmers than anticipated taking part.
The push for legalization was driven by the medical uses of cannabis. The cannabis plant contains more than one hundred cannabinoids. The best known is THC, which alters the taker's perception, concentration and sense of time, but can also trigger mental health problems. CBD, by contrast, has calming, relaxing, and anti-inflammatory effects without causing intoxication.
The legal pharmaceutical production of cannabis is subject to strict regulations, mandatory quality standards, and comprehensive inspections - requirements that discourage many small-scale farmers.
At the same time, there is widespread distrust of state institutions. Many people complain about arbitrary treatment and corruption. Police officers who profit from the illegal trade undermine the implementation of the reforms. 
This documentary explores the promises and pitfalls of cannabis legalization for Morocco's cannabis-growing communities - where the debate itself often divides generations and even families.

items.title: What Gravitational Waves Reveal About the Universe, with Michelle Thaller
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Go to https://ground.news/startalk to stay fully informed on the latest Space and Science news. Save 40% off through our link for unlimited access to the Vantage plan this month.

Could spacetime curve in the opposite direction and produce a repulsive field instead of gravity? Neil deGrasse Tyson and comic co-host Chuck Nice tackle fan questions about photons, heat death, gravitational waves, neutron stars and more with astrophysicist Michelle Thaller.

The episode opens with an urgent conversation about NASA funding cuts and the exodus of top scientists and engineers leaving for overseas programs. We get into fan questions: what actually happens to a photon when it's absorbed and reemitted? Does it restart its journey through spacetime with a new identity? What is the heat death of the universe, and will matter eventually run out? Why does temperature increase as you move away from the sun's surface? We answer these and also get into what the Parker Solar Probe is teaching us about the sun.

We explore gravitation and whether it can be inverted. Michelle uses the question to walk through how LIGO detected gravitational waves from two black holes colliding 1.4 billion light years away, capturing the most energetic event in the universe.

We explore neutron stars, fast radio bursts, and the first generation of stars the James Webb Space Telescope is hunting for. Learn how the mysterious "little red dots" may rewrite our understanding of how the earliest stars formed. Michelle closes with a message for young girls considering science: you don't need a special kind of genius, you just need to be unable to get it out of your head. Keep Looking Up!

items.title: You should be thinking differently about the midterm elections
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>There are two ways of looking at the current divides within the Democratic Party. The first — and more dominant — narrative is that the party’s left wing is on an upward march.

The second explanation is that the party is rudderless — an ideological fight to be settled in the next presidential election — and that the left’s success in New York City, Colorado, and even Maine (before Graham Platner’s campaign collapsed) grows out of a void left by a bigger, less-talked-about story: an establishment in free fall, on the wrong side of fundamental shifts across its own rank-and-file base.

items.content:
<article>Sean Illing talks with neuroscientist Gregory Berns, author of The Self Delusion. Berns claims that the idea of a unified, persistent self is a kind of illusion, and that we are better understood as multiple selves at different moments in time, tied together by a story — which is what we call our identity. Sean and Greg also talk about whether the brain is a computer, how perception works, the limits of thinking too much about thinking, and what psychedelics can do to disrupt and change the stories we tell about ourselves.

items.title: Will non-alcoholic wine save the winemakers? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Wine consumption is declining in Europe. This poses a threat to European wine-growing regions. Winemakers in Spain and Germany are seeking a way out of the crisis by producing alcohol-free wine.

Many people want to live healthier lives. As a result, alcohol consumption in Europe has declined: by a good 20 percent, over the past 20 years. It’s a trend that also impacts wine: Experts warn that nearly a third of Germany’s vineyard acreage could disappear in the coming years. Particularly affected are the labor-intensive steep slopes. These slopes produce distinctive wines, shape the cultural landscape and attract tourists.

Jürgen and Luca Dahms share their love of wine. Yet their perspectives also diverge. Father Jürgen, a winemaker, stands for classic, traditional wine enjoyment, while Luca, who works in the insurance industry, has found surprising success marketing alcohol-free wines. Both see an opportunity to preserve threatened vineyards by de-alcoholizing wines. 

In Spain, in the historic wine region of Toro, winemaker Iván Alonso Gil is undertaking a bold experiment. His full-bodied red wines come from ancient vines. Can they still taste great without alcohol? Iván is having a few bottles of his wine de-alcoholized in Germany using a special process that includes aroma recovery. But will he recognize his own wine afterward? And could this be a project for the future?

items.title: Baby eels worth billions | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The European glass eel is critically endangered. It's also one of the most smuggled animals in the world. The global black market for baby eels is worth more than 2.5 billion euros. Part of what makes them so valuable is that eels can't be bred commercially in captivity. Every glass eel entering the trade has to be caught in the wild. Scientists still don't fully understand the conditions under which eels reproduce. Adult eels are believed to spawn in the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic Ocean, and their young swim more than 5,000 km across the Atlantic to Europe's rivers and lakes. The conditions under which eels mate and produce offspring remain difficult to study and have not yet been successfully replicated in captivity. 

Watch the full documentary "On the smugglers' trail - Making billions from tiny eels" on the DW Documentary YouTube channel.

items.content:
<article>For decades, Pakistan has grappled with one crisis after another. The Kashmir conflict with India repeatedly escalates into military exchanges of fire. Economic stagnation is fueling social frustration.

For decades, India and Pakistan, two South Asian nuclear-armed neighbors, have been locked in a bitter struggle over the Himalayan region of Kashmir. The Line of Control, the ceasefire line between the two powers, is considered one of the most dangerous borders in the world.
 
But Pakistan's challenges do not come only from outside: radical Islamists in parts of the country continue to launch attacks on security forces and civilians. Some Islamist clerics even call on their followers to oppose the Pakistani state. The Pakistani military has launched several operations to quell the unrest.
 
Of Pakistan's 240 million people, 47 percent are under the age of 18. Yet, economic stagnation and a weak education system are fueling frustration among the country’s young and rapidly growing population.
 
Against this backdrop, the military has considerably expanded its influence in what political analysts say is a "hybrid" system of governance with elected civilian representatives. The military continues to play a major role in the country's politics and economy. While the human rights organizations criticize the army's role in politics, the military officials point to various security challenges that, in their view, require their involvement.

items.title: Where Did Venezuela's $13 Billion Go?
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>If you’re looking to upgrade your business wardrobe, I can recommend giving Tailor Store a try. Their shirts are made to your measurements, so you can create something that fits both your body and your personal style. My viewers receive 25% off their first order through my link: https://www.tailorstore.com/patrickboyle

When the United States took control of Venezuela's oil exports in early 2026, it collected an estimated $13 billion in crude sales — but the official ledger in Caracas records almost none of it, and six months on there is still no public accounting of where the money went. In this video we look at what happened to Venezuela's sovereign wealth: the missing oil revenues now sitting in an offshore account in Qatar, the four billion dollars of Venezuelan gold frozen in the vaults of the Bank of England that no one can legally claim, and the court-ordered auction that handed Citgo's parent company to an affiliate of Paul Singer's Elliott Management for nearly $6 billion. Along the way we explain the legal machinery that makes all of this possible — the alter ego doctrine, sovereign immunity and the Bancec ruling, the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, and the "one voice" principle in English law — and the broader lesson for anyone trying to understand sovereign assets: a nation's wealth held abroad is only yours for as long as someone else's courts, banks and vaults agree that it is. We also cover the aftermath of the June earthquakes, the international relief effort, and why the question of who legitimately governs Venezuela sits at the centre of every one of these disputes.
